name: Question Quest
topics_techniques_covered: receptive_vocabulary: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Shown a strange, intriguing picture, the child asks as many questions about it as they can and guesses what caused it and what might happen next.
interaction: An odd scene appears (a door in a tree, a puddle that glows). The child builds questions by tapping starter cards (Who / What / Where / Why / How / What if) and finishing them, or types them freely; separate rounds invite 'guess why this happened' and 'guess what happens next.' The engine logs the number of questions, their depth (surface what/who vs causal why/how vs hypothetical what-if), and the fluency and variety of the cause and consequence guesses. Every question and guess is welcomed; none is wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the scene, then a hand tapping the 'Why...?' card and a question bubble popping up, then a 'What if...?' card with another bubble - cueing 'ask lots of questions about it.' One unscored warm-up scene lets the child ask two questions before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Ask-and-guess (asking questions and guessing causes and consequences about a picture) is a validated divergent-thinking task
learning_science.why: It elicits question generation and hypothesis generation - forms of ideational fluency that alternate-uses and consequences prompts do not directly sample
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score fluency and variety of the child's questions and guesses about an intriguing stimulus rather than a single keyed answer
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Spontaneous question-asking is a direct behavioral index of epistemic curiosity and drives learning
learning_science.why: The rate and depth of a child's questions during a novel activity reflect an intrinsic drive to close information gaps that reasoning tests cannot see
learning_science.concrete_decision: Count questions and rate their depth (surface fact vs causal vs hypothetical) as the curiosity signal (M-QUERY) instead of a curiosity questionnaire
learning_science.source: Engel, S. (2011). Children's need to know: Curiosity in schools. Harvard Educational Review, 81(4), 625-645.

learning_science.principle: Children's questions are a mechanism for gathering information and building knowledge
learning_science.why: Information-seeking questions, especially causal ones, mark active knowledge construction and predict who pursues understanding on their own
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distinguish information-seeking causal/explanatory questions from mere labeling questions when scoring depth
learning_science.source: Chouinard, M. M. (2007). Children's questions: A mechanism for cognitive development. Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development, 72(1), 1-129.

tail_precision_rationale: CogAT observes what a child does when told exactly what to do; it never observes the questions a child asks when facing the unknown. M-QUERY (count and depth of questions) is a direct epistemic-curiosity axis, and grading question depth - causal/hypothetical over labeling - separates children who probe mechanism from those who merely name. The guess rounds add M-IDEAFLU, M-FLEX (variety of causal and consequential explanations), and M-ORIG (rare-but-plausible guesses) so the same activity yields both a curiosity and a divergent-thinking signal. At the gifted tail this distinguishes an able-but-incurious child from an able-and-inquisitive one, and it does so through question generation rather than the physical exploration and uncertainty-choice mechanic of the Mystery Box. M-ENGAGE confirms questioning reflects interest, not idle tapping.
age_rationale: Composing questions on screen depends on emerging question syntax and enough language to fill starter cards, more reliable from about grade 2; K-1 curiosity is captured behaviorally by the tactile Mystery Box instead. From grade 2 up, starter-card scaffolds support 2-3 while 4-5 and 6-8 compose freely, and prompts are voiced for early readers. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: simple single-oddity scenes (young) up to rich scenes with many possible questions and subtler anomalies (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: scene complexity and ambiguity, number of embedded anomalies, whether cause and consequence guessing is required, question-window length
adaptive.notes: Difficulty is depth of possible inquiry, not correctness: branch to richer, more ambiguous scenes for children who ask many deep questions so the ceiling of inquiry is probed rather than a theta on accuracy.

engagement_hook: A mysterious scene that begs 'what is going on here?', where every question the child asks lights up the picture and reveals a tiny hint - curiosity is immediately rewarded with a peek behind the mystery.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Question quantity confounds with verbal ability and question syntax (use starter-card scaffolds and voicing; score depth, not word count); shy or reticent children may under-ask even when curious (corroborate with the Mystery Box behavioral signals); scene-content familiarity shapes what feels puzzling (rotate novel scenes); depth rating of questions can be subjective (use a clear causal-vs-labeling rubric and audit). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: What Would You Do?
topics_techniques_covered: inference_reading_comprehension: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: A short animated scene shows a tricky social or school situation, and the child taps the character action they think works best (then sees what happens next).
interaction: An illustrated/animated scenario plays (voiced for pre-readers), pausing to offer 2-4 pictured action choices. The child taps a choice; the scene branches to show a consequence, sometimes leading to a follow-up decision. Responses are keyed against an expert-consensus effectiveness scale (partial credit for good-but-not-best options). The engine logs choice, decision time, how long options are inspected before choosing, and any changes of mind.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a scene of a dropped lunch tray, a hand tapping the 'help pick it up' character over the 'walk away' character, and a happy outcome - cueing 'tap the best thing the character could do.' One unscored warm-up scenario is played and discussed with a neutral outcome before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Situational judgment tests validly assess practical/social judgment via response to realistic scenarios
learning_science.why: Judgment and social-emotional competence predict adjustment and achievement but are untouched by abstract reasoning items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use branching scenario items keyed to an expert-consensus effectiveness scale (partial credit) rather than a single right answer
learning_science.source: McDaniel, M. A., Morgeson, F. P., Finnegan, E. B., Campion, M. A., & Braverman, E. P. (2001). Use of situational judgment tests to predict job performance. Journal of Applied Psychology, 86(4), 730-740.

learning_science.principle: Task-approach judgment (how one handles hard, boring, or frustrating work) reflects conscientiousness and self-regulation
learning_science.why: A child who chooses persistence/help-seeking strategies in scenarios reveals dispositions that predict school success
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include conscientiousness scenarios ('your project is hard and boring - what do you do?') scored for effective self-regulatory choices
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., & Seligman, M. E. P. (2005). Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents. Psychological Science, 16(12), 939-944.

learning_science.principle: Animated, low-reading situational judgment can assess young children's social decision-making in a game
learning_science.why: Interactive branching scenarios reduce the reading load and increase ecological validity for social-emotional skills
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver scenarios as voiced animations with pictured choices and branching consequences (stealth SEL) for K-1
learning_science.source: DeRosier, M. E., & Thomas, J. M. (2019). Establishing the criterion validity of Zoo U's game-based social-emotional skills assessment. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment, 37(3), 341-354.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning cutoffs ignore social/practical judgment entirely. Keying scenarios to an expert-consensus scale yields a graded score (M-POLY) rather than dichotomous right/wrong, extracting tail information from each rich item. M-PATH and M-EXPLORE (which options and branches the child inspects before committing) plus decision time (M-RT) reveal deliberate weighing versus impulsive choosing, and M-CONF calibration down-weights lucky picks. Together these add a judgment axis that separates equally 'able' children by the quality and deliberateness of their real-world decisions.
age_rationale: Voiced animation with pictured choices makes scenarios fully accessible to non-readers (K-1); text and richer branching are layered in for 4-5 and 6-8. Tapping a character is the only motor demand, appropriate for all bands. (D-017: K-1 removed — its K-1 access depended on audio narration of language the child must comprehend; with audio prohibited and reading required, the floor rises to grade 2.)

adaptive.content_range: simple one-step social scenes (young) up to multi-step branching dilemmas with competing goods (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of branches, subtlety of the best option, competing considerations, delay between action and consequence
adaptive.notes: Branching is intrinsic: the chosen action determines the next scene, so difficulty adapts by routing stronger judges into subtler follow-up dilemmas. Scoring is consensus-keyed rather than a pure ability theta.

engagement_hook: A choose-your-own-adventure story where the child's tap changes what happens next, making social judgment feel like steering a cartoon rather than answering a quiz.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Scenario choices are semi-self-report and thus fakeable/social-desirability-prone (children may pick the 'nice' answer they think adults want) - mitigate with behavioral timing, forced trade-offs between two goods, and consequence branching; cultural norms shape 'best' responses (localize consensus keys and audit for bias); reading load must stay low via voicing; expert-consensus keys can encode rater bias (use diverse expert panels). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Claim Duel
topics_techniques_covered: verbal_reasoning_argumentation: the child builds a position by matching the strongest evidence to a claim and rebuts opposing arguments, scored on claim-evidence link quality (Argubot-style argumentation)
inference_reading_comprehension: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child props up a claim by dragging the strongest evidence cards to it and knocks down a rival claim by picking its weakest link.
interaction: A claim card is shown with a pool of evidence cards (some strongly relevant, some weakly/irrelevantly related, some off-topic). The child taps evidence cards to attach them to the claim, building the strongest support; then in a duel a rival claim appears and the child taps the evidence that best rebuts it. Strength meters fill by link quality. Picture/icon-supported cards with short audio labels keep reading load low. No typing.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps the on-topic strong-evidence card onto the claim (its strength bar fills green) and skips the off-topic card (which greys out) - under 10s, showing attach strong evidence, not weak. One unscored warm-up with one clearly strong and one clearly irrelevant card runs before scored, subtler items begin.

learning_science.why: Strong arguments link claims to data via warrants; recognising and building those links is the core of argumentation skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cards are typed as claim, evidence (strong/weak) and warrant so the child's attachments are scored against argument structure, not surface agreement.
learning_science.source: Toulmin, S. E. (1958). The Uses of Argument. Cambridge University Press.

learning_science.principle: Argument skill as coordinating claims and counterclaims
learning_science.why: Mature reasoning evaluates evidence and integrates counterarguments rather than only supporting one's own view.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The rebuttal phase requires attacking the rival claim's weakest evidence, measuring evaluation of counterclaims not just one-sided support.
learning_science.source: Kuhn, D. (1991). The Skills of Argument. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY (graded claim-evidence link quality) extracts multiple bits of tail information from one rich item, and M-LURETYPE reveals whether errors are pulled by thematic-associate or weak-but-related lures, grading discrimination of evidential relevance. M-PATH preserves the attach/rebut sequence for evidence-model scoring of argument construction, while M-RTFIRST and M-REV separate deliberate evidence evaluation from surface matching.
age_rationale: Coordinating claims with supporting versus irrelevant evidence, and evaluating a counter-claim, requires emerging metacognitive argument skills generally accessible from 4-5 with concrete, picture-supported topics, extending to 6-8 with abstract claims, subtler lures and multi-card warrants. Below 4-5 explicit claim-evidence coordination is developmentally limited, setting the floor; audio labels keep reading load low. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: one-strong-one-irrelevant concrete claims (4-5) up to abstract claims with subtle weak-but-related lures and multi-step warrants (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: evidence-relevance subtlety (strong vs weak vs thematic lure)
requirement to supply a warrant linking data to claim
adaptive.notes: Claim/evidence sets are templated with relevance-tagged cards and lure classes for M-LURETYPE; strong topical variety needs curation, so cloning is moderate.

engagement_hook: A friendly debate duel where strong evidence powers up your side and rebuttals knock down the rival makes reasoning feel like a battle, driving effortful evaluation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Picture-plus-audio cards keep reading load low; tap-to-attach removes typing; cards are typed by evidential role so scoring reflects link quality not opinion agreement; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; topics are kept culturally neutral and non-controversial so background knowledge does not confound the reasoning score. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Fib Finder
topics_techniques_covered: listening_comprehension_inference: the child listens to a short spoken argument and infers whether the conclusion follows and where it breaks, scored on the inference depth caught
verbal_reasoning_argumentation: the child evaluates a claim-and-reason and locates the unsupported step or false premise
verbal_absurdities: at easy levels the child spots an impossible or foolish statement in the spoken passage
one_liner: The child listens to a short spoken reason-and-claim and taps the part that does not make sense or the step that does not follow.
interaction: A character speaks a two or three line argument (for example, all birds can fly, so a penguin can fly to the tree). The scene shows two to three tappable picture cards, each standing for one spoken statement or the conclusion; the child taps the card that is wrong or does not follow. A REPLAY button re-plays the audio. The correct choice lights up. Difficulty scales from silly absurdities to subtle logical gaps. No reading; all statements are spoken with picture cues.
self_teach: The ghost-hand listens to a fish riding a bicycle to school, then taps the fish-on-bicycle card which shakes as silly - under 10s, showing tap the part that cannot be true. One unscored warm-up on an obvious absurdity runs before scored, subtler flawed-reasoning items begin.

learning_science.why: Mature verbal reasoning evaluates whether a conclusion actually follows from its reasons rather than only agreeing with it.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must locate the unsupported step or false premise, so the score reflects argument evaluation not opinion.
learning_science.source: Kuhn, D. (1991). The Skills of Argument. Cambridge University Press.

learning_science.principle: Listening comprehension in the Simple View of Reading
learning_science.why: Delivering the argument by ear isolates language comprehension and inference from decoding ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Full audio with picture cards lets pre-readers show comprehension and flaw detection.
learning_science.source: Gough, P. B., & Tunmer, W. E. (1986). Decoding, reading, and reading disability. Remedial and Special Education 7(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-INFDEPTH (deepest flaw layer detected: impossible fact, then invalid inference, then subtle unsupported warrant) is the sharpest tail separator because verbal-reasoning discrimination is about how subtle a gap a child can catch. M-LURETYPE reads whether errors are pulled by the plausible-but-irrelevant statement and M-HINT (replays) adds a dynamic-assessment signal.
age_rationale: Spotting an obvious spoken absurdity with picture cards is accessible from 2-3. 4-5 adds simple does-not-follow reasoning; 6-8 adds subtle unsupported warrants and near-valid arguments that separate strong verbal reasoners. Audio delivery with picture cards means no reading at any band. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: obvious absurdities (2-3) up to subtle unsupported-warrant arguments (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Argument skeletons are templated with flaw-type-tagged statements and lure classes; new spoken lines need audio generation so cloning is moderate.

engagement_hook: Playing a fib-catching detective who spots the silly or sneaky part of what a character says makes critical listening feel like a game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Full audio plus picture cards removes reading load; replays are logged as hint use not blocked; flaws are designed by type not trickery; topics are kept culturally neutral so background knowledge does not confound reasoning; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Word Forge
topics_techniques_covered: orthographic_lexical_access: the child forms as many valid words as possible from given letter tiles under a time budget, indexing lexical access speed and orthographic knowledge (anagram/word-building)
one_liner: The child taps letter tiles to build as many real words as they can before the sand timer runs out.
interaction: A rack of letter tiles is shown. The child taps letters to spell a word into a slot then taps ENTER; valid words score and animate onto a shelf while invalid strings gently shake and clear. Longer and rarer words earn brighter gems. A visible sand timer bounds the round. Tiles can be reused across words. Letters are voiced on tap to support emerging readers. No keyboard typing (tap-to-build only).
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps C-A-T then ENTER; the word flies onto the shelf with a chime, then taps C-A-T-S for a bigger gem - under 10s, showing build words, longer is better. One unscored warm-up round on an easy rack runs before the scored, timed round begins.

learning_science.why: Fluent readers rapidly connect letter strings to known words; speed and breadth of this access is a strong verbal-ability marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring rewards number, length and rarity of valid words produced under time, indexing orthographic-lexical access rather than handwriting or spelling dictation.
learning_science.source: Ehri, L. C. (2005). Learning to read words: Theory, findings, and issues. Scientific Studies of Reading 9(2).

learning_science.principle: Productive fluency as an ability signal
learning_science.why: Open production (generate many valid items) lowers the ceiling and reveals verbal breadth beyond recognition items.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child produces words freely rather than selecting from options, so fluency and lexical depth separate the tail; letter audio lowers the decoding barrier.
learning_science.source: Carroll, J. B. (1993). Human Cognitive Abilities: A Survey of Factor-Analytic Studies. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-IDEAFLU (count of distinct valid words) and M-VOCABLVL (rarest word-frequency band produced) are ceiling-resistant fluency and lexical-depth signals that keep separating strong verbal children after common short words are exhausted. M-RTFIRST (time to first valid word) and inter-word latency index lexical-access speed, while M-FLEX (variety of word length/root families) distinguishes deep lexicons from repetitive stems.
age_rationale: Building short words from tiles with letter audio is accessible once basic letter-sound knowledge emerges (2-3), with easy high-frequency racks. 4-5 adds longer racks and length bonuses; 6-8 uses racks that afford rare/long words and tighter timers that reward deep lexical access. Tap-to-build avoids handwriting/keyboard demands. Below 2-3 letter knowledge is generally insufficient, setting the floor. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: short high-frequency word racks (2-3) up to racks affording long/rare words under tight time (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: letter set (how many long/rare words it affords)
adaptive.notes: Racks are generated against a frequency-tagged lexicon that guarantees a known set of valid words for scoring M-IDEAFLU and M-VOCABLVL; unlimited parallel racks matched on solution count.

engagement_hook: Forging words into glowing gems against a sand timer is a satisfying race, and chasing longer/rarer words for bigger gems drives effortful production.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Letters are voiced on tap so decoding does not block emerging readers; tap-to-build removes handwriting/keyboard motor load; the validated lexicon avoids penalising legitimate rare words; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; scoring weights breadth and rarity over raw speed so thoughtful producers are not penalised. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Letter Climb
topics_techniques_covered: orthographic_lexical_access: the child changes one letter at a time to climb from a start word to a goal word, each rung a real word, indexing rapid access to the orthographic lexicon and word neighbourhoods
one_liner: The child changes one letter at a time to climb from the start word to the goal word, each rung a real word.
interaction: A start word (for example CAT) and a length-matched goal word are shown as letter tiles; the child taps a letter position then taps a new letter to change exactly one letter, forming the next word, which must be a real word (valid words lock in as a rung; invalid strings gently shake). The ladder grows until the goal is reached in as few rungs as possible. Letters are voiced on tap. No keyboard typing.
self_teach: The ghost-hand turns CAT into COT by changing one letter, which locks as a rung, then COT into COG - under 10s, showing change one letter to make a new word and climb. One unscored warm-up (one change reaches the goal) runs before scored ladders begin.

learning_science.why: Finding a valid neighbour word by a single letter change requires rapid access to the orthographic lexicon, a strong verbal-ability marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each rung must be a real word, so the task indexes orthographic-lexical access and neighbourhood knowledge not handwriting.
learning_science.source: Ehri, L. C. (2005). Learning to read words: Theory, findings, and issues. Scientific Studies of Reading 9(2).

learning_science.principle: Search efficiency in a constrained word space
learning_science.why: Reaching the goal in few rungs rewards planful lexical search over random letter changes.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Rungs-over-minimum is scored so efficient lexical pathfinding is credited.
learning_science.source: Newell, A., & Simon, H. A. (1972). Human Problem Solving. Prentice-Hall.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (rungs versus the shortest ladder) is a continuous ceiling-resistant separator of lexical pathfinding and M-VOCABLVL captures the rarity of the intermediate words a child can access. M-RTFIRST and inter-rung latency index lexical-access speed while M-PATH preserves the full ladder for strategy scoring.
age_rationale: Changing one letter to make a new word needs emerging spelling and decoding, so it starts at 4-5 with short high-frequency three-letter ladders and letter audio. 6-8 uses longer words, longer minimum ladders and rarer intermediate words that reward deep lexical access. Below 4-5 letter-word knowledge is generally insufficient, setting the floor. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: short three-letter one-change ladders (4-5) up to longer words with long minimum ladders and rare rungs (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Ladders are generated against a frequency-tagged lexicon with a shortest-path solver for M-EFF and M-VOCABLVL and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Climbing a word ladder one letter at a time toward the goal word is a classic puzzle with fewest-rungs stars that reward clever routes.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Letters are voiced on tap so decoding does not block emerging readers; tap-to-change removes handwriting and keyboard load; the validated lexicon accepts legitimate rare words; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; rung efficiency and breadth not raw speed are scored. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Build-It Buddy
one_liner: Listen to step-by-step spoken directions and build the picture by dragging, placing, and coloring the pieces so it matches what was described.
interaction: An empty canvas plus a tray of pieces (shapes, animals, colors) is shown while audio gives a multi-step construction direction (put the red square in the top corner, then put a star under it, then color the tree green). The child performs each step by dragging a piece to a location, placing it, or tapping a color; a replay repeats the audio once. Unlike selection tasks the child constructs the arrangement from scratch. Steps lock on submit and are auto-scored against the described end-state as partial credit; the number of steps and embedded conditions adapt up after success (an above-grade span staircase).
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): audio gives a two-step direction and the hand drags a red circle to the box then puts a star on top, matching a briefly shown target. One unscored warm-up (put the sun in the sky) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Executing multi-step spoken directions that place and modify objects (put the red circle on the green square) is a validated receptive-language and verbal-working-memory index, and construction rather than selection removes recognition shortcuts.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Directions require building an arrangement from an empty canvas, scored step-by-step against the end-state, with an adaptive step and condition count (M-ORALSPAN, M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: De Renzi, E., & Vignolo, L. A. (1962). The Token Test: A sensitive test to detect receptive disturbances in aphasics. Brain, 85(4), 665-678.

learning_science.why: Holding an ordered set of construction steps while executing them taxes updating and sequencing, a strong reasoning- and executive-linked signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Steps are delivered in one spoken pass with a single replay so the maximum ordered steps executed indexes span rather than re-listening.
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. (1992). Working memory. Science, 255(5044), 556-559.

learning_science.why: A spoken direction paired with a manipulable visual canvas lets the child map language onto action with no reading, keeping the task near-language-neutral for pre-readers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: All directions are audio and all responses are drag/place/color actions on pictures; a caption fallback and replay protect against audio and attention noise.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Construction turns one direction into a graded, multi-step item: partial credit (M-POLY) for steps satisfied plus the adaptive oral-direction step/condition span (M-ORALSPAN, M-DIFFREACH) drive each child to the maximum ordered spoken constraints they can hold and execute (a sharp tail separator because gifted children carry 4-5 embedded steps). The action log (M-PATH) shows whether they build systematically in the described order, and re-placements (M-REV) separate decisive builders from trial-and-error at the cut.
age_rationale: A one- or two-step build with large pieces is within K-1 motor and attention range; more steps, embedded conditions, and color/relational modifiers extend to 6-8. No reading at any band (audio plus one replay); drag/place/color on large targets keeps motor demand modest and revisions are logged so fumbles are not scored as comprehension errors. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: One- or two-step placements of large pieces (K-1) up to multi-step directions with embedded spatial, relational, and color conditions (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of steps; embedded conditions per step; relational and spatial complexity; piece count on the tray; single replay allowed
adaptive.notes: A grammar-templated construction-direction generator over a tagged piece/canvas library; each step auto-scored against the target end-state; parallel forms swap same-band pieces and layouts.

engagement_hook: A build-along craft game where following the spoken plan makes a little scene assemble itself piece by piece; finishing a long plan reveals a completed picture like following a treasure map.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Loads verbal working memory alongside comprehension (one replay caps memory-only failure; reported with WM and separated from motor via M-REV/M-PATH); drag precision is a motor demand (large snap targets, place-not-type); audio clarity (caption fallback plus replay in the demo); language background (dialect-neutral, frequency-leveled direction wording); construction adds a light visual-planning load kept modest by capped piece counts per band. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Fill the Gap
one_liner: Complete a sentence with the missing idea by picking the picture or word that best fills the gap.
interaction: A sentence is presented with a blank (audio with a beep at the gap plus pictures for young; a printed sentence with a blank plus word choices for older). The child taps the best option; it drops into the blank and the full sentence plays/reads back. Context-clue items require using the rest of the sentence; a scrambled-tiles variant asks the child to drag words into a meaningful order.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the dog wants to ___ plays with pictures (bone / car / cloud); the hand taps the bone, it slots into the blank, and the sentence replays. One unscored warm-up runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Filling a deleted element measures integration of syntactic and semantic context, a validated comprehension and language-proficiency index.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Gaps are placed so only contextual reasoning (not a single collocation) selects the answer; distractors fit locally but not globally.
learning_science.source: Taylor, W. L. (1953). Cloze procedure: A new tool for measuring readability. Journalism Quarterly, 30(4), 415-433.

learning_science.why: Using surrounding context to infer the right word is a hallmark of strong verbal reasoning and predicts vocabulary growth.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Higher bands include low-frequency target words recoverable only from context (M-VOCABLVL + M-INFDEPTH).
learning_science.source: Sternberg, R. J. (1987). Most vocabulary is learned from context. In M. G. McKeown & M. E. Curtis (Eds.), The Nature of Vocabulary Acquisition (pp. 89-105). Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Oral sentence + picture completion lets pre-readers show sentence reasoning with no print.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio sentence frames with picture options; printed cloze appears only from 4-5 up.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Context-recoverable low-frequency targets make this a joint vocabulary-by-inference tail probe: M-VOCABLVL captures the rarity of words a child can pin from context and M-INFDEPTH captures whether they used global sentence meaning versus a local collocation. Parallel matched gaps (M-CONSIST) tighten the standard error right at the cut, and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) flags reflective integration over guess-and-check.
age_rationale: Oral sentence completion with picture answers is valid at K-1 (no reading); printed cloze with context clues extends to 6-8. Single tap; reading load only in the older printed mode, offset by an audio option. (D-017: K-1 removed — its K-1 access depended on audio narration of language the child must comprehend; with audio prohibited and reading required, the floor rises to grade 2.)

adaptive.content_range: Simple oral sentence + picture completion -> multi-clause cloze requiring global context and rare target words; a scrambled-order variant covers sentence arrangement.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: context distance (local vs whole-sentence); target word frequency; syntactic complexity; picture vs word; number of options.
adaptive.notes: Sentence-frame bank with gap slots; distractors auto-tagged local-fit vs global-fit; the scrambled-order variant supports sentence_arrangement.

engagement_hook: A missing-puzzle-piece snap: the right piece clicks into the sentence and the scene it describes comes alive (the dog actually chews the bone).
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence completion is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by audio for young bands, frequency leveling, and ELL-neutral frames); local-collocation shortcuts (mitigated by global-fit-only gaps with local-fit lures); reading load at older bands (audio option); single-tap motor. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Proof Hunt
one_liner: Answer a question about a short story, then tap the exact part that proves your answer.
interaction: A short passage is shown (audio + 3-4 comic panels for pre-readers; printed text split into tappable sentences for older bands). Step A: an inference/main-idea question appears with picture or text choices and the child taps an answer. Step B: the child taps the sentence(s) - or the comic panel - that is the evidence for that answer; selected text highlights and can be toggled off. Submit locks both parts. Scored as a two-part evidence-based selected response: full credit needs the right answer AND the right evidence.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a two-panel scene plays (a child holds an empty lunchbox and frowns); the question shows two faces, the hand taps the hungry face, then glides to the empty-lunchbox panel and taps it so it glows as the 'proof'. One unscored warm-up runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Requiring the child to locate the supporting evidence, not just pick an answer, forces them to ground inferences in the text and blocks lucky guessing, which is the modern standard for valid reading-comprehension measurement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every scored item is two-part: an inference answer plus a required text-or-panel evidence selection, scored together as partial credit (M-POLY).
learning_science.source: Smarter Balanced Assessment Consortium (2015). Evidence-Based Selected-Response and Technology-Enhanced Item Specifications for English Language Arts.

learning_science.why: Selecting correct evidence for an inference requires linking a conclusion back to the propositions that license it, exposing the coherence of the child's mental model rather than verbatim memory.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Answer distractors are surface-text matches while evidence distractors are true-but-irrelevant sentences, so only a coherent model selects both correctly.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

learning_science.why: Comprehension discrimination at the tail is about inference layer (literal -> bridging -> global -> author's purpose), so grading the depth of the question a child can support with evidence separates strong comprehenders.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Questions are tagged by inference depth and the deepest layer supported with correct evidence is recorded (M-INFDEPTH).
learning_science.source: Cain, K., & Oakhill, J. (1999). Inference making ability and its relation to comprehension failure. Reading and Writing, 11(5), 489-503.

tail_precision_rationale: Requiring evidence turns one comprehension item into a two-part partial-credit item (M-POLY): answer-only credit versus answer-plus-evidence separates children who truly grounded the inference from those who guessed. M-INFDEPTH records the deepest inference layer a child can support with correct evidence, and M-PATH (which sentences were tapped, in what order) plus M-ERRTYPE (chose a plausible-but-unsupported sentence vs an off-topic one) reveal near-misses that mark latent ability just under the cut.
age_rationale: A pre-reader version uses an audio story with 3-4 comic panels where 'evidence' is tapping the panel that shows the proof, so it works at K-1 with a single tap and no reading; from 2-3 up the passage becomes tappable printed sentences (highlight-the-proof), with longer text and deeper inference layers through 6-8. Reading load at older bands is offset by a read-aloud option. (D-017: K-1 removed — its K-1 access depended on audio narration of language the child must comprehend; with audio prohibited and reading required, the floor rises to grade 2.)

adaptive.content_range: Two-panel picture stories with one-step inference (K-1) up to multi-paragraph literary/informational passages needing global or author's-purpose inference and multi-sentence evidence (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: passage length; inference depth (literal -> bridging -> global -> author's purpose); number of evidence sentences required; strength of the plausible-but-unsupported evidence lure; listening vs reading.
adaptive.notes: Passages are human-curated but question+evidence sets and lure sentences are templatable; parallel forms swap matched-difficulty passages.

engagement_hook: A detective mechanic: answering is 'making the accusation' and highlighting the evidence 'proves the case' - the passage flashes a magnifying-glass stamp and a 'Case Solved' badge only when answer and proof agree.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading decoding can confound comprehension at older bands (mitigated by a listen mode and by the picture-panel evidence version for young bands); highlighting UI could add motor/selection noise (large sentence hit-boxes, toggle-to-deselect, revisions logged via M-REV/M-PATH); background knowledge (balanced, novel-world topics); the evidence step is language-light (tap, not type) to protect ELL children. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Two Meanings
topics_techniques_covered: antonyms_synonyms: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Hear a word that has two meanings inside a spoken sentence, then tap the picture that shows the meaning the sentence points to.
interaction: A homograph is shown and a sentence using it is read aloud (and printed for readers). Four pictures appear: the sentence-appropriate meaning, the OTHER meaning of the same word, a thematic associate, and an unrelated foil. One tap selects; the correct meaning then lights green.
self_teach: Wordless demo: 'The BAT flew around the dark cave' plays while a ghost hand taps the flying-bat picture (green) and the baseball-bat picture stays grey; one unscored warm-up before scoring. Audio + pictures mean no reading is needed.

learning_science.why: Selecting a word's meaning from sentence context indexes semantic control and comprehension monitoring beyond raw vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty lever is context-bias strength and whether the biased meaning is dominant or subordinate; the OTHER-meaning picture is always present as the key competitor.
learning_science.source: Swinney, D. (1979). Lexical access during sentence comprehension. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior.

learning_science.why: Forcing the subordinate meaning taxes controlled retrieval, the tail-relevant skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Later levels bias the less-frequent meaning so strong comprehenders who suppress the dominant reading are separated.
learning_science.source: Rodd, J., Gaskell, G. & Marslen-Wilson, W. (2002). Making sense of semantic ambiguity. Journal of Memory and Language.

learning_science.why: Spoken sentence + pictures removes decoding load so the task self-teaches.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ghost-hand demo + one unscored trial; audio is replayable.
learning_science.source: Mayer, R. (2005). Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning (modality principle).

tail_precision_rationale: Mapping bias strength to inference depth (M-INFDEPTH: strong-literal up to subtle-subordinate) records the deepest disambiguation a child sustains, which keeps separating strong comprehenders after literal items ceiling. Because the OTHER-meaning picture is always present, choosing it (vs an associate or unrelated foil) is a diagnostic near-miss (M-LURETYPE/M-ERRTYPE) that localizes latent ability just below the cut; an adaptive frequency staircase (M-VOCABLVL/M-DIFFREACH) individualizes the frontier.
age_rationale: Spoken sentence + picture choice is accessible to pre-readers (K-1) with high-frequency homographs and strong context; subtle context and subordinate, low-frequency meanings extend the ceiling to 6-8. (D-017: K-1 removed — its K-1 access depended on audio narration of language the child must comprehend; with audio prohibited and reading required, the floor rises to grade 2.)

adaptive.content_range: concrete high-frequency homographs (bat, bark, ring) with strong context up to low-frequency words with subtle/subordinate-meaning context
adaptive.difficulty_levers: context-bias strength; dominant vs subordinate target meaning; word frequency; similarity of the associate lure
adaptive.notes: Clone by pairing a homograph with a meaning-biasing sentence frame and four tagged pictures; needs a curated homograph+picture bank (picture availability limits full auto-generation).

engagement_hook: One word, two secret meanings - be the detective who catches which one the sentence really means.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Picture recognizability (use clear, culturally neutral images); listening load (short, replayable sentences); vocabulary exposure (frequency-level words, support with audio); ensure exactly one picture fits the sentence so the key is unambiguous. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Relation Match
one_liner: See how one pair of words goes together, then pick the OTHER pair that goes together in the very same way.
interaction: A key pair is shown (audio + pictures for young; printed frequency-leveled words for older), for example bird -> nest. Below are three or four candidate PAIRS; the child taps the pair whose relationship matches the key pair's (bee -> hive), not one that is merely associated. The chosen pair links to the key with an animated relation arc and locks. This is relation classification (matching a relationship) rather than completing A:B::C:?.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the key pair bird -> nest lights with an arc; the hand hovers each candidate pair, rejects dog -> bone (wrong relation), and taps bee -> hive so a matching arc glows. One unscored warm-up (key fish -> water; pick bird -> sky) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Selecting the pair that shares a relation is pure relational alignment with surface content varied, so it isolates relational reasoning from single-word vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Candidate pairs are built so one shares the key relation while distractors share only an associate or surface link, forcing relation (not theme) matching.
learning_science.source: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155-170.

learning_science.why: Children move from matching on surface/associative similarity to matching on relational similarity; which basis a child uses is a graded index of relational maturity and reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors include an associative lure (thematically related but wrong relation) so the response reveals whether the child matches relationally or associatively (M-LURETYPE).
learning_science.source: Gentner, D., & Rattermann, M. J. (1991). Language and the career of similarity. In Perspectives on Language and Thought (pp. 225-277). Cambridge University Press.

learning_science.why: Zero written instructions and a single animated relation arc keep working memory on the relationship rather than on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The relation arc externalizes the mapping and there is no instructional text; young bands use pictures with audio labels.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Matching relations across varied surface content isolates fluid relational-verbal reasoning at the cut. The lure taxonomy (M-LURETYPE / M-ERRTYPE: associate lure vs surface-match lure vs reversed-relation lure) reveals whether a near-miss reflects associative capture (surface reasoning) or a subtle relational confusion (latent ability just under threshold); candidate-sampling (M-EXPLORE) and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) separate decisive relational matchers from those who compare pairs one-by-one, adding process resolution beyond accuracy.
age_rationale: Matching a familiar relation between picture pairs is within K-1 grasp (single tap, no reading, audio labels); raising relation abstractness and switching to printed frequency-leveled words extends it to 6-8. Motor demand is one tap throughout. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: One concrete relation among picture pairs (animal->home) up to abstract or double relations among low-frequency printed word pairs.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation abstractness; number of candidate pairs; strength of the associative lure; picture vs printed word; word frequency.
adaptive.notes: AIG from a relation-typed pair bank; distractor pairs auto-selected as associate, surface-match, and reversed-relation lures; parallel forms swap same-band pairs.

engagement_hook: A matchmaker game: draw a glowing arc between the two pairs that belong together the same way; the right match sparks and locks, an associate trap fizzles.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Relation familiarity can carry culture (mitigated by universal relations for young bands and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST); associative distractors must be calibrated so they mislead by reasoning, not by unfamiliarity; reading load only in the word mode (frequency leveling + audio option); single-tap motor keeps motor noise low. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Sentence Sense
one_liner: Drag the scrambled word cards into order to build the sentence that makes sense - not the silly one that breaks the rules of the world.
interaction: Word cards (picture-plus-word for young bands with audio labels; frequency-leveled printed words for older) appear scrambled on a rack. The child drags them into a track to form a sentence. The same words can form more than one grammatical order, but only one is sensible (the cat chased the mouse) while the other is absurd (the pizza ate the boy is impossible, or the mouse chased the cat is world-implausible in the framed scene); the child must build the sensible one. An optional second tap on the leftover silly reading marks why it is silly. Cards snap into slots, can be re-dragged (a revision), and lock on submit; scoring credits adjacent-pair order plus semantic plausibility.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three scrambled cards (chased / cat / mouse with a the) are dragged into the cat chased the mouse and the scene plays it out; the reversed silly order wobbles and is rejected. One unscored warm-up (dog / the / barks) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Arranging words into a grammatical sentence taps productive syntactic knowledge that comprehension-only items miss and that scales with syntactic complexity such as embedding and clauses.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cards are arranged into a track and scored on word order, with complexity raised by adding clauses rather than rare words.
learning_science.source: Semel, E., Wiig, E. H., & Secord, W. A. (2003). Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fourth Edition (CELF-4): Sentence Assembly. Pearson.

learning_science.why: Choosing the sensible ordering over a grammatical-but-absurd one forces integration of the sentence against world knowledge, the Verbal Absurdities construct, so syntax and meaning are jointly probed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each item admits a grammatical absurd ordering as a lure so only a child who checks plausibility (not just grammar) scores full credit; the absurd reading is tagged for M-ERRTYPE.
learning_science.source: Kutas, M., & Hillyard, S. A. (1980). Reading senseless sentences: Brain potentials reflect semantic incongruity. Science, 207(4427), 203-205.

learning_science.why: A drag-to-order mechanic with a played-out scene self-teaches and keeps working memory on sentence logic, not on task instructions or decoding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 and 2-3 use picture-plus-audio cards and large drag targets with no instructional text; the assembled sentence is animated so meaning is verified visually.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Ordering yields graded credit (M-POLY by adjacent-pair correctness), turning one item into many bits, while the plausibility contrast adds inference depth (M-INFDEPTH: did the child reject a grammatical-but-absurd reading) that pure arrangement misses. The drag log (M-PATH) and re-drags (M-REV) separate decisive planners from shufflers, and M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a grammatical-but-silly ordering (semantic near-miss, latent ability) from an ungrammatical scramble, sharpening placement at the cut.
age_rationale: Arranging three picture-plus-audio cards is within 2-3 reach (large drag targets, no reading); printed word cards, longer sentences, added clauses, and subtler plausibility violations extend to 6-8. K-1 word-order building is heavier than a single tap so it is carried by tap-based verbal types and this type starts at 2-3 by design; dragging (not typing) keeps expressive load low. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: 3 picture-plus-audio cards forming a simple SVO sentence (2-3) up to 6-8 word printed cards forming multi-clause sentences with a grammatical-but-absurd lure (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of cards; syntactic complexity (SVO to embedded clauses); closeness of the absurd ordering to the sensible one; picture-plus-audio versus printed word; word frequency leveled so rare vocabulary does not confound syntax
adaptive.notes: Sentence frames generate scrambles plus a grammatical-but-implausible lure ordering; distractor orderings tagged ungrammatical versus grammatical-absurd; parallel forms swap same-band frames and same-frequency words.

engagement_hook: A word-builder where snapping the cards into the sensible order makes the scene come alive and act it out, while the silly order makes a goofy impossible cartoon - so getting it right is the funny payoff.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence building is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by picture-plus-audio cards for young bands, frequency leveling so syntax not rare vocabulary carries difficulty, and ELL-neutral frames); world-knowledge plausibility can be cultural (universal physical and biological scenarios); drag motor demand (large snap slots, free re-dragging, M-REV logged so fumbles are not scored as errors); reading load only in the older printed mode (audio labels available). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Story Order
one_liner: Put the mixed-up parts of a story in the right order, then choose what happens next.
interaction: Three to six story parts appear scrambled - picture panels for pre-readers, sentence strips for older bands. The child drags them into a track to make the events make sense (temporal/causal order). When ordered, a 'what happens next?' probe offers picture or text choices; a 'why did it happen?' probe may also appear. Submit locks the order and the prediction. The order is auto-scored by how many pairs are in the correct relative order.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three panels (plant a seed / water it / flower blooms) sit scrambled; the hand drags them into 1-2-3 order, then a 'next?' card shows a bee visiting and the hand taps it. One unscored warm-up (wake up / eat breakfast / go to school) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Reconstructing event order requires representing goals, causes, and consequences (story grammar); success indexes causal-temporal inference beyond word reading.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Panels/strips are ordered by causal necessity, not just clock time, so correct sequencing requires inferring cause-effect links.
learning_science.source: Stein, N. L., & Glenn, C. G. (1979). An analysis of story comprehension in elementary school children. In R. O. Freedle (Ed.), New Directions in Discourse Processing. Ablex.

learning_science.why: Predicting what happens next from a reconstructed sequence is forward causal inference, a hallmark of strong comprehenders and a probe standard tests rarely score interactively.
learning_science.concrete_decision: After ordering, a prediction probe and an optional 'why' probe are graded by inference depth (M-INFDEPTH) as partial credit.
learning_science.source: Cain, K., & Oakhill, J. (1999). Inference making ability and its relation to comprehension failure. Reading and Writing, 11(5), 489-503.

learning_science.why: A drag-to-order mechanic with picture panels teaches itself and lets pre-readers show causal reasoning with zero print, keeping working memory on the story logic.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses wordless picture panels and large drag targets; no instructional text at any band.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Ordering yields graded credit (M-POLY: number of correctly ordered pairs / Kendall-tau), turning one item into many bits of information, and the prediction + why probes add M-INFDEPTH (causal vs surface). The drag log (M-PATH) plus efficiency (M-EFF: moves vs the minimum needed) and revisions (M-REV) separate children who plan the causal chain and place decisively from those who shuffle by trial-and-error, adding process resolution exactly at the cut.
age_rationale: Wordless three-panel picture sequencing with large drag targets is within K-1 motor/attention range; strip count, causal subtlety, and a shift to sentence strips (which also carries sentence_arrangement) raise it through 6-8. Dragging (not typing) keeps expressive-language and reading load low; a read-aloud option covers decoding at older bands. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: 3 wordless picture panels in obvious time order (K-1) up to 5-6 sentence strips ordered by causal necessity with a global 'why' inference (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of parts; time-order vs causal-order; similarity/interchangeability of parts; picture vs sentence strips; presence of prediction and 'why' probes.
adaptive.notes: Event-chain templates generate scrambles and near-order distractors; curated art/sentences per chain; parallel forms swap matched chains.

engagement_hook: A comic-strip studio: snap the panels into a filmstrip and it 'plays' the little movie when the order is right, then you guess the next frame - reordering feels like storytelling, not testing.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Drag precision is a motor demand (large targets, snap-to-slot, free reordering, M-REV logged so motor fumbles are not scored as errors); reading load only in the sentence-strip mode (audio option, picture mode for young); working-memory load of holding the chain (kept modest by limiting parts by band); culturally balanced, universal event chains. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Sorting Robot
one_liner: Watch a robot drop a few example pictures or words into its IN bin or OUT bin, figure out the hidden category rule, then sort new items IN or OUT yourself.
interaction: A friendly robot has a green IN bin and a red OUT bin. It first demonstrates by dropping two or three labeled examples - positive examples fall IN, negative examples fall OUT - revealing a hidden semantic category (for example, animals go IN and non-animals go OUT). Then new item cards are handed to the child one at a time; the child taps IN or OUT (or drags the card into a bin). An optional 'peek' lets the child test one example to see where the robot files it (a scored hint). Correct sorts snap with a chime and the robot's happy meter fills; the round ends after a fixed set. Audio names each item for pre-readers; older bands use frequency-leveled printed words and more abstract, superordinate, or functional categories. This is category-rule induction from examples, not picking a fourth member or ejecting an odd one.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): the robot drops a dog IN, an apple OUT, and a cat IN (the hidden rule is 'animals'); a new fish card appears and the hand taps the IN bin so it snaps in. Then one unscored warm-up round (hidden rule 'round things') runs with feedback before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Inducing a category from positive and negative examples and testing candidates against the inferred rule is core inductive classification, exposing concept formation rather than mere recognition of a named group.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each round hides one semantic rule; the demonstrated examples are the positive/negative evidence and the child's sorts of new items reveal the induced rule; the test sequence is logged (M-EXPLORE).
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. S., Goodnow, J. J., & Austin, G. A. (1956). A Study of Thinking. Wiley.

learning_science.why: Semantic categories are organized around prototypes with graded membership, so using near-boundary exemplars probes the structure and precision of a child's concepts independent of expressive language.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Test items include clear central members plus near-boundary and competing-category lures so correct sorting requires precise category boundaries; young bands use universal, prototypical picture categories.
learning_science.source: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192-233.

learning_science.why: How quickly a child converges on the hidden rule from feedback is a dynamic-assessment signal (learning rate) that adds tail validity beyond a static accuracy score and resists coaching.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Trials-to-criterion and the reduction in the viable-rule space per sort are scored as hypothesis-search efficiency (M-HYP), and optional peeks are logged (M-HINT) so hint-free fast induction is credited more.
learning_science.source: Grigorenko, E. L., & Sternberg, R. J. (1998). Dynamic testing. Psychological Bulletin, 124(1), 75-111.

tail_precision_rationale: Rule induction turns one classification round into a learning curve: M-HYP (trials-to-criterion / viable-rule-space reduction) captures how fast a child infers the hidden category, a dynamic-assessment tail separator beyond static accuracy, while M-EXPLORE and M-HINT distinguish systematic testers from guessers and credit hint-free induction. M-DIFFREACH escalates category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/superordinate) to the child's edge, and M-ERRTYPE flags boundary near-misses (fine category discrimination, latent ability just under the cut) versus random misfiles.
age_rationale: IN/OUT sorting of obvious picture categories with audio labels and a single tap is within K-1 reach; abstract, superordinate, and functional categories with printed frequency-leveled words extend it through 6-8. No reading at young bands (audio); the response is a single tap or a large-target drag, and the demonstrated examples stay on screen so working-memory load of the rule is kept modest. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: Concrete taxonomic categories such as animals vs non-animals (K-1) up to abstract/superordinate and functional or cross-domain word categories (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/superordinate); closeness of boundary exemplars and competing-category lures; number of demonstrated examples before testing; picture vs printed word; word frequency (Zipf band).
adaptive.notes: AIG from category-tagged picture/word banks; positive and negative demonstration exemplars plus near-boundary and competing-category lures auto-selected; parallel forms swap same-abstractness categories and same-frequency words.

engagement_hook: A friendly robot that is 'thinking' of a secret rule; cracking the rule and feeding it the right items fills its happy meter and makes it beep with delight, so figuring out the robot's secret is the game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Category knowledge can reflect exposure and culture (mitigated by universal, prototypical categories and audio-plus-picture for young bands, frequency leveling for words, and dropping low-fit items via matched parallels); reading load only in the word mode (frequency leveling plus audio labels); single-tap or large-target drag keeps motor noise low; the on-screen demonstration examples cap the working-memory load so the task measures induction, not memory. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Word Train
topics_techniques_covered: verbal_classification: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Drag the scrambled word cars onto the train track in the right order to build one correct, meaningful sentence.
interaction: Scrambled word cars sit on a platform (picture-plus-audio word cars for young bands; frequency-leveled printed words for older). The child drags them onto a track to form a grammatical sentence; the engine plays the sentence aloud when the order is meaningful. A recognition variant instead offers four candidate orderings and the child taps the correct one. Syntactic complexity rises with success (simple subject-verb-object up to embedded clauses) while word frequency is leveled so rare vocabulary never carries difficulty; cars re-drag freely (a revision) and lock on submit, scored by adjacent-pair and whole-order correctness.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three scrambled cars (runs / the / dog) are dragged into the dog runs and the train chugs off reading it aloud. One unscored warm-up (a / nap / cat / the with an audio target) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Ordering words into a grammatical sentence taps productive syntactic competence that recognition items miss, and syntactic difficulty (clauses, embedding) provides a high ceiling for able children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cars are arranged on a track and scored on word order, with difficulty raised by syntactic structure rather than rare vocabulary.
learning_science.source: Semel, E., Wiig, E. H., & Secord, W. A. (2003). Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, Fourth Edition (CELF-4): Sentence Assembly. Pearson.

learning_science.why: Building complex (especially embedded) sentences loads verbal working memory, and individual differences in that capacity separate strong from average syntactic processors.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Complexity is scaled by embedding depth and clause count, and the highest structure a child orders correctly is recorded (M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: King, J., & Just, M. A. (1991). Individual differences in syntactic processing: The role of working memory. Journal of Memory and Language, 30(5), 580-602.

learning_science.why: If rare words carried difficulty the task would measure vocabulary and print exposure, not syntax; leveling word frequency isolates the arrangement construct and lowers ELL bias.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Words are drawn from the child's frequency band via a Zipf staircase (M-VOCABLVL) and audio labels are provided so decoding does not gate syntax.
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

tail_precision_rationale: Word order is scored as graded credit (M-POLY by adjacent-pair correctness / Kendall tau), so one item yields many bits and near-misses (one transposition) score above scrambles. The highest syntactic structure ordered correctly (M-DIFFREACH) is an above-grade ceiling index, efficiency versus the minimum moves (M-EFF) and the drag path (M-PATH) separate planful builders from trial-and-error, and frequency leveling (M-VOCABLVL) guarantees the signal is syntax, not rare-word knowledge, right at the cut.
age_rationale: Ordering three picture-plus-audio word cars is within 2-3 reach with large drag targets and no reading; printed words, longer sentences, and embedded clauses extend to 6-8. K-1 multi-card ordering exceeds a single tap so it is carried by tap-based verbal types; dragging (not typing) keeps expressive load low and a read-aloud option offsets decoding at older bands. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: 3 picture-plus-audio cars forming a simple subject-verb sentence (2-3) up to 7-plus printed cars forming multi-clause sentences (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of cars; syntactic complexity (SVO to embedded and relative clauses); distractor orderings in the recognition variant; picture-plus-audio versus printed word; frequency band of the words
adaptive.notes: Sentence frames generate scrambles and near-order distractors; word frequency is a native staircase and syntactic templates give unlimited matched parallel forms.

engagement_hook: A train-building game where the word cars only chug away once the sentence is in the right order; longer, fancier sentences pull a longer, cooler train.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence arrangement is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by picture-plus-audio cars for young bands, frequency leveling so syntax not rare vocabulary carries difficulty via M-VOCABLVL, and ELL-neutral frames); reading load only in the older printed mode (audio labels and read-aloud); drag motor demand (large snap slots, free re-dragging so fumbles are not scored as errors); working-memory load of holding the target sentence is kept modest by band-limited length. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Bubble Pop Memory (n-back / dual n-back)
one_liner: Bubbles float up one at a time showing a picture, and the child taps POP whenever the current bubble matches the one from n bubbles ago; a dual mode adds a sound channel.
interaction: Bubbles rise at a fixed pace, each showing a shape or colour; the child taps a POP button when the current bubble equals the one n steps back (single stream). Dual mode plays a chime or shows a letter alongside each bubble with a separate SOUND-POP button, and the child responds to either channel independently. Taps do not advance the stream. n rises when signal-detection sensitivity is high (about 80 percent) and falls when it is low, pushing each child above grade level; scoring is sensitivity- and consistency-based, never raw speed.
self_teach: A wordless 1-back ghost-hand demo shows two identical bubbles in a row and the hand tapping POP with a check (about 6s), then an unscored 1-back warm-up; the rising-bubble rhythm and the POP button read instantly with no text.

learning_science.principle: N-back as a continuous updating measure
learning_science.why: The n-back requires constant encoding, monitoring, and replacement of working-memory contents and correlates with fluid reasoning, giving a high ceiling as n rises.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a continuous rising-bubble stream with a POP judgment and an adaptive n level that escalates above grade.
learning_science.source: Kirchner, W. K. (1958). Age differences in short-term retention of rapidly changing information. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 55(4), 352-358.

learning_science.why: Adding a second modality stream raises domain-general updating demand and lifts the ceiling for older children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a dual visual-plus-auditory mode with separate response buttons per channel for the 6-8 band.
learning_science.source: Jaeggi, S. M., Buschkuehl, M., Jonides, J., & Perrig, W. J. (2008). Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 105(19), 6829-6833.

learning_science.why: Hits and false alarms confound ability with response bias unless modeled with sensitivity, so consistency and d-prime rather than hit count define the score.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score with d-prime and flag lure (n plus or minus 1) false alarms rather than crediting fast taps.
learning_science.source: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. A. (1966). Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics. Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: A continuous updating stream is rich in tail telemetry: signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) separates true match detection from response bias, lure false alarms (M-FALSEALARM at n plus or minus 1) expose fragile temporal binding, the accuracy-by-load slope (M-UPDATECOST) indexes updating efficiency, and the highest sustained n (M-DIFFREACH) probes capacity above grade level; RT variability (M-RTVAR) scores worst-performance consistency rather than impulsive speed.
age_rationale: Continuous updating with response withholding is too demanding for most K-1 children, so the floor is 2-3 (single 1-back at a gentle pace), rising to 2-3-back at 4-5 and dual-channel n-back at 6-8. Only one or two large buttons are tapped and the sound channel has a visible letter fallback so audio is not required. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 single 1-back at a gentle pace up to 6-8 dual visual-plus-auditory n-back at higher n
adaptive.difficulty_levers: n level; single versus dual channel; bubble pace; target and lure rate
adaptive.notes: Bubble streams, tones, and lure schedules are generated with controlled target and lure rates, and n is a native above-grade staircase.

engagement_hook: A bubble-popping arcade where you pop only the bubbles that repeat from n-ago; faster streams and a second sound channel make leveling up feel like a real challenge.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention and ADHD are the dominant confound: continuous updating loads sustained attention and impulse control, so bias-free d-prime is reported, consistency is weighted over speed, and scores are gated on engaged blocks. A fixed pace can clip slow responses (generous response window). Novelty is mitigated by the warm-up. The auditory channel uses a visible letter so muted or deaf and hard-of-hearing children are not disadvantaged. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Word Machines
topics_techniques_covered: receptive_vocabulary: the child maps a written word to the picture it denotes, but the entire lexicon is invented, so what is probed is a mapping being built inside the block rather than one the child arrived with — which is the point, because in verbal the standing failure mode is that any learning measure collapses into crystallized vocabulary
